sense: raise to a higher rank or post

evidence: Liv. 39.40.5: ad summōs honōrēs aliōs scientia jūris … prōvexit
Cic. Phil. 13.24: ecquō tē tua virtūs prōvexisset?
terms.comment: To carry forward, and so to raise someone to a higher post (Lewis & Short). In the passive it is also to sail out, and to be carried away (longius prōvehī, to go too far).

evidence: Plin. Ep. 7.31.3: prōmōtus ad amplissimās prōcūrātiōnēs (Lewis & Short)
Traupman 187: ad (in) ampliōrem gradum prōmovēre, promote to a higher rank
Traupman 31: ad superiōrem classem prōmovēre, to promote (a pupil) to the next class
terms.comment: In this sense post-Augustan (Curtius, Pliny, Suetonius); classically to move forward, push on (Caes. BC 2.11, Lewis & Short).
Late Latin (Lewis & Short); classical Latin uses the verb: prōvectus est, he was promoted.

phrases.latin: ad summōs honōrēs aliōs scientia jūris, aliōs ēloquentia, aliōs glōria mīlitāris prōvexit
phrases.english: some men were raised to the highest offices by their knowledge of law, some by their eloquence, some by their fame as soldiers

phrases.latin: ecquō tē tua virtūs prōvexisset, ecquō genus vītae?
phrases.english: how far would your own merit have got you, or your way of life?

sources: Lewis & Short: proveho · Lewis & Short: promoveo · Lewis & Short: promotio
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 187, 365, 31 (promote; promotion).
Livy and Cicero checked against the Latin Library texts (CLTK mirror) (11 November 2026).
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, with its references, in the house spelling (macrons, consonantal j); they have not been checked against a modern edition.

short-o.claim: short o in the present stem
short-o.html: The simple verb is mŏveō in Lewis & Short; the long ō belongs to the perfect mōvī and the participle mōtus, and the compound keeps the short vowel of the present.
